Nika Gvaramia interview

World.title: Opinion: ‘Removing Kobakhidze would be logical move for Ivanishvili if prime minister does not move against him first’
World.content:
Opinion on Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze

According to Eka Gigauri, executive director of Transparency International Georgia, removing Prime Minister Kobakhidze could eventually become a logical step for Ivanishvili — provided the prime minister does not manage to seize political power himself.

Eka Gigauri: “The Garibashvili case has once again confirmed what we already knew:”

None of this has anything to do with fighting corruption. Ivanishvili is reshuffling his inner circle, while Kobakhidze — with his approval and Mdinaradze’s assistance — is getting rid of political rivals. In “Georgian Dream”, no one is surprised when people enrich themselves at the public’s expense or engage in corruption: they all steal. The entire system is built on corruption, and Ivanishvili gave them the freedom to do so. So the “fight against corruption” is merely a staged performance designed to conceal a settling of scores. Kobakhidze does not get his hands dirty himself. He has Mdinaradze to do that for him, who has become his loyal executor and servant. It is obvious that the overwhelming majority of “Georgian Dream” supporters genuinely support Garibashvili. The same cannot be said of Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze. Look at the reactions from “Dream” supporters to statements by Garibashvili and his wife. If the authorities imprisoned Mdinaradze and then Kobakhidze, “Dream” supporters would not say a word in their defence. To them, Kobakhidze is still a former NGO worker and employee of international organisations. He is not a churchgoer and has no particular ties to the Church. The same applies to much of his team. There is no friendship, brotherhood or willingness to support one another in the “Georgian Dream” party. Apparently, none of them possesses that quintessential Georgian sense of honour. Out of fear of Bidzina, and now of Kobakhidze as well, they will betray one another, throw each other under the bus and abandon one another in times of trouble. Ivanishvili is deliberately deepening divisions within his own team and turning its members against one another. His goal is to prevent them from uniting against him and to force them to constantly undermine and confront each other. Today, Kobakhidze is clearly Ivanishvili’s favourite. However, he appears to have been carried away by this status. He often talks about his personal achievements, as though he had the power to act even without Ivanishvili. He may not have many genuine supporters within “Georgian Dream”, but today he exercises almost complete control over state institutions. “Georgian Dream” members appear to fear Kobakhidze greatly — perhaps even more than Bidzina. They know that Kobakhidze has direct access to Bidzina and can tell him something about a fellow party member that could ultimately destroy them. Even Garibashvili did not have this kind of influence. Kobakhidze has placed his people almost everywhere, while parliament is under his complete control. He has gradually concentrated enormous power in his hands. If this continues, even Ivanishvili may find it difficult to dismantle the system.

The experience of authoritarian regimes around the world also shows that dictators manage their inner circles according to the principle of “divide and rule”. They periodically replace their favourites and involve everyone in corruption schemes and other crimes, so that they can later use their weaknesses and complicity against them. At the same time, they pit influential groups against one another and keep everyone in a constant state of fear through selective punishment.

Thus, no individual or group can accumulate enough power to pose a real threat to the leader. However, such a system also carries a significant risk: a favourite who has concentrated all the levers of power in their hands may eventually begin building an independent political force. That is why dictators often get rid of their most loyal and influential allies.

At the same time, members of an authoritarian ruler’s inner circle often initiate changes of power. In other words, autocrats and dictators have good reason to fear their own inner circles. Today, if Kobakhidze wanted to, he could even remove Bidzina, and no one in “Georgian Dream” would dare oppose him. Therefore, removing Kobakhidze would eventually become a perfectly logical step — unless he managed to remove Ivanishvili first.

Opinion on Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze

World.title: ‘We are not on our knees, we are fighting for justice’: David Babayan’s message from Baku prison
World.content:
David Babayan’s message from a Baku prison

“What kind of trial was it? It was a theatrical performance, with the script written in advance,” David Babayan, the former foreign minister of the former unrecognised Nagorno-Karabakh Republic, said in a message from a Baku prison.

Babayan’s family gave the audio recording of his message to an Armenian media outlet. In his message, he discusses the trial of the former NKR’s military and political leadership. Two weeks ago, the Court of Appeal upheld the verdicts handed down by the Baku Military Court. In February 2026, David Babayan received a life sentence. He described the Court of Appeal’s ruling as a “formal stage” that had to be completed before the case could be taken to an international court.

“One interesting development was that one of the defence lawyers here [at the Baku court] said they did not want the case to reach an international court because more than 95% of the charges were fabricated and there was no evidence. That is exactly what happened,” Babayan said.

He also said that he and other prisoners were facing serious health problems. He stressed that despite their difficult situation, they were fighting for justice, freedom and human rights.

“It is one thing to fight and stand up for justice, and another to sit in prison for it. But know this: although we are imprisoned, we are not on our knees,” Babayan concluded.

On 5 February 2026, the Baku Military Court sentenced former president Arayik Harutyunyan, Defence Army commander Levon Mnatsakanyan, deputy commander Davit Manukyan, parliament speaker Davit Ishkhanyan and foreign minister David Babayan to life imprisonment. The court sentenced former presidents Arkady Ghukasyan and Bako Sahakyan to 20 years in prison. Baku brought serious charges against all the defendants, ranging from terrorism to genocide. The two former presidents received shorter sentences because of their age. Under Azerbaijani law, courts cannot sentence people over 65 to life imprisonment. The case of former state minister Ruben Vardanyan was heard separately. On 17 February, a Baku court sentenced him to 20 years in prison.

Falsifications instead of evidence

“Remarkably, instead of evidence, they use substitutes here: lies, falsifications, toasts, various political approaches, slogans and so on.

We pointed out that the legal system and the courts cannot operate like the food or chemical industries, where people use substitutes.

Nothing can replace facts and evidence.

But that is how things work in this court. And that is their general approach to us.

Moreover, these falsifications and lies remain in their archives. At times, we tried to see how they recorded all this in their documents. We found that they had not included our statements at all or, at best, had included heavily shortened or distorted versions. This is nothing other than legal apartheid.”

On the old and new charges against him

“What is happening here is simply unimaginable. For example, they automatically attribute a crime committed by one person to everyone.

They added two life-sentence charges to my case that had never appeared before and had never been mentioned throughout the entire first-instance trial. I noticed this when they gave us a brief summary a week after the trial ended. This is unacceptable.

I asked them to review our statements — both my final statement at the first-instance trial and the main statements we made during this trial — and provide them in video format to Azerbaijan’s human rights ombudsman. But they refused.

They say the trial is open, but refuse to provide all the information even to their own human rights ombudsman.

One interesting phenomenon was that five or six defence lawyers changed during this period. One of them changed at the very beginning of the appeal proceedings. I tried to find out why. They told me it was because of health problems. During the hearing, I said: ‘Contact him by video. I want to ask him about his health personally.’ Of course, they became uncomfortable and did not put us in contact. They said his life was not in danger.

They sentenced me to life imprisonment under an article alleging that I had tried to seize power here [in Azerbaijan] and overthrow the constitutional order.

I asked whether there was any evidence that I had taken part in a struggle for power while I was here. If that were the case, I would have had supporters across your country and cells belonging to some organisation. Of course, I received no answer.

The court accepted 100% of our complaints in favour of the prosecution. At the first-instance trial, 99.4% of them went in favour of the prosecution.

I thanked them for mistakes of such quality and quantity because they are very important for us. They will help justice prevail because we will present all of this to an international court.”

Selected groups of people were brought to the hearings on special buses

“There were no Azerbaijani citizens at the Court of Appeal hearings, whereas the first-instance trial always had around 200-300 people in attendance.

Of course, they selected all of them specifically and brought them in on special buses. We saw this.

According to some reports, they were also paid well. But no one attended this trial.

One reason is that these people saw the abuses that took place there. They saw the weak position of their own side, our independent defence, our persistence and the quality of our self-defence. Naturally, whether they wanted it or not, all this information reached their society. That is why they banned these people from attending.”

David Babayan’s message from a Baku prison

World.title: A Gal-Media TV station building has burned down in Abkhazia
World.content:
In Abkhazia, a building housing the regional TV company Gal-Media has been destroyed by fire. Without their equipment, journalists now plan to film their reports using smartphones.

The TV company, which serves the predominantly ethnic Georgian Gali district, occupied several rooms in a four-storey building. The fire destroyed the editing room, recording room and studio where the main news bulletins were produced. It also destroyed all the studio equipment, the server room and the entire archive.

Security camera footage helped investigators identify the exact point where the fire started. It broke out near the ceiling, where a layer of soundproofing foam had been installed. Specialists believe an old bundle of electrical wiring may have caused the fire. Although the premises underwent renovations in 2016, workers did not replace this old section of wiring.

Gali district administration head Konstantin Pilia said emergency services were investigating the incident and expected to release their findings in the coming days. Specialists are also assessing the extent of the damage and the cost of repairs and replacement equipment. The district and republican authorities have already begun taking steps to restore the TV station’s operations.

Because of the fire, Gal-Media will continue operating on a limited basis. Journalists will temporarily use their surviving personal smartphones and laptops to prepare reports. This will allow them to publish information on social media. However, the station’s regular analogue broadcasts will be suspended for the time being, Gal-Media head Thea Arshba said.

The Gali district administration is already looking for temporary premises for the TV company’s staff while repairs are under way.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Gal-Media TV station premises destroyed by fire in Abkhazia

World.title: From C5 to C6: how Azerbaijan is reshaping balance of power in Central Asia
World.content:
Azerbaijan at Central Asia’s table

On 16 November 2025, the five Central Asian states accepted Azerbaijan as a full member of the Consultative Meeting of Heads of State. Eight months later, on 31 July, Ilham Aliyev took his place at the table at an informal summit in Cholpon-Ata not as a guest, but as one of six equal participants.

The format is now officially known as “Central Asia and Azerbaijan”. The term “C6” has already entered expert vocabulary and is being used at conferences.

The change expands Central Asia’s political and economic cooperation to the western shore of the Caspian Sea. It also turns Azerbaijan from an external partner into a full participant in a route connecting the region with Turkey and Europe.

How did the format emerge and why has it expanded?

Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev proposed the idea of a consultative mechanism at the UN in September 2017. The first meeting took place in Astana on 15 March 2018. The format’s advantage was its simplicity: without a treaty, permanent secretariat or supranational bodies, the leaders of the five countries could directly discuss borders, water resources, trade and security.

Azerbaijan did not join the process immediately. Ilham Aliyev attended meetings in Dushanbe in 2023, Astana in 2024 and Tashkent in 2025 as an honorary guest. Since the beginning of 2023, he has visited Central Asian countries 16 times, while the region’s leaders have travelled to Azerbaijan 26 times. In 2025, Azerbaijan’s trade with the five Central Asian states grew by 53% to $1.8 billion. Trade among the Central Asian countries themselves reached $10.7 billion in 2024.

Mirziyoyev described Baku’s accession as an opportunity to create a “single space for cooperation” between Central Asia and the South Caucasus. Aliyev, in turn, described the two shores of the Caspian as a “single geopolitical and geoeconomic space”.

The leaders of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan said they supported expanding the format because it would create new opportunities for transit, logistics and energy cooperation.

The Middle Corridor and the Caspian’s role in bringing the region together

The geography offers the clearest explanation for Azerbaijan’s participation in the format. The Middle Corridor links China and Central Asia with Europe: goods travel by rail across Kazakhstan to the ports of Aktau and Kuryk, then across the Caspian Sea to Alat, before continuing through Georgia towards Turkey and the Black Sea. Azerbaijan effectively serves as the western gateway to the route.

According to the Kazakh government, freight volumes along the Trans-Caspian route rose by 62% in 2024 to 4.5 million tonnes. Baku says the volume of cargo travelling through the Azerbaijani section of the Middle Corridor has increased by 90% over three years. The authorities plan to raise the capacity of the Port of Alat to 25 million tonnes a year. The World Bank estimates that if countries coordinate border procedures, tariffs, port operations and transport schedules, freight volumes along the corridor could triple by 2030, while delivery times could fall by half.

The plans go beyond container shipping. Proposed electricity and digital cable projects across the Caspian would also bring energy and information flows into the broader agenda of regional cooperation.

The route through Nakhchivan offers new opportunities but remains contentious. The Washington Declaration, signed on 8 August 2025, provides for a transport link through Armenia between mainland Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan, based on the sovereignty and jurisdiction of the states concerned, as well as the development of the TRIPP mechanism. Baku calls the route the “Zangezur Corridor”.

If implemented, the route could give the Middle Corridor an additional link to Turkey. However, until the parties agree on customs procedures, security arrangements, financing and management mechanisms, it remains a project rather than an operational transport corridor.

What is changing from a geopolitical perspective?

“C6” is a convenient political label, not the official name of an organisation. The format remains a consultative platform based on consensus. It does not involve collective defence commitments or mechanisms to enforce decisions.

For Moscow, this is therefore primarily about competition over logistics and political influence, including through the development of routes that bypass Russia, rather than the emergence of a new military alliance.

Beijing gains an additional route to the west and more stable conditions for transit.

Ankara has an interest in strengthening direct transport links across the Caspian.

The European Union and the US see the format as an opportunity to reduce dependence on routes through Russia and expand access to Central Asia.

The new C6 format should not be confused with the Organisation of Turkic States. The OTS has a treaty-based framework and institutional cooperation among Turkic states. The “Central Asia and Azerbaijan” format also includes Tajikistan and focuses less on shared identity than on geography, economic interests and regional cooperation.

Potential opportunities and real constraints

The potential areas for cooperation are quite concrete: common transit tariffs, digital customs procedures, coordinated port and railway schedules, joint investment funds, green energy exports, tourism routes and coordination at international forums. With its ports, financial resources and transport links through the Caucasus and Turkey, Azerbaijan offers Central Asian countries additional routes and opportunities. Baku, in turn, gains more systematic access to the region’s five markets and their economic ties with China.

However, there are also many constraints. The six countries differ in their economic potential, interests in water resources and energy, and priorities in their relations with Russia, China, Turkey and the West. The format has no permanent secretariat or mechanisms to enforce decisions, so implementation of political agreements will depend on intergovernmental coordination.

The Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea, signed in 2018, has yet to be ratified by Iran, while delimiting the seabed requires separate agreements. Falling water levels in the Caspian, the shallowing of ports and the need for costly dredging also increase the environmental and economic costs of transport logistics.

From symbol to concrete projects?

Mirziyoyev has already proposed transforming the format into a “Community of Central Asia” with a rotating secretariat. The next official meeting, scheduled for 8 October 2026 in Avaza, will be one of the first tests of whether these intentions can turn into practical decisions.

Will the six countries agree on common tariffs, digital customs procedures and a stable ferry schedule? Will TRIPP become a fully fledged part of the Middle Corridor without creating new border disputes? Or will the “Central Asia and Azerbaijan” format remain a flexible consultative platform, with its informal nature continuing to be its main advantage?

Azerbaijan at Central Asia’s table

World.title: Singapore's Changi Airport Group keen to co-op with Kazakhstan on Astana airport project
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. Singaporean Changi Airport Group (CAG) is interested in further deepening cooperation with Kazakhstan, particularly in the implementation of the project to construct a new airport in Astana, the Kazakh Prime Minister's press service reported.

The issue was addressed during a meeting between Kazakh Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and Changi Airport Group CEO Yam Kum Weng. The sides discussed prospects for cooperation in the aviation sector.

"Yam Kum Weng expressed Changi Airport Group's interest in further deepening cooperation with Kazakhstan. The head of the Singaporean company noted Astana's significant potential as a bridge between Europe and Asia and confirmed the group's readiness to provide its expertise, knowledge and experience in the airport sector for the implementation of the project to construct a new airport in the capital as a regional hub", the government said.

Bektenov noted that, in line with instructions from Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev to establish an international aviation hub, comprehensive work is underway to develop Astana's airport infrastructure, including the construction of a second airport.

He noted the significant potential for expanding practical cooperation between Kazakhstan and Singapore and emphasized the importance of attracting international experience and the company's technological expertise to the development of Kazakhstan's aviation infrastructure.

Following the meeting, the sides confirmed the high level of Kazakhstan-Singapore relations and expressed interest in further expanding practical cooperation.

The sides noted that further cooperation could focus on creating a comprehensive airport ecosystem in Kazakhstan.

Changi Airport Group operates Singapore's Changi International Airport and Seletar Airport. Through its subsidiary Changi Airports International, the group participates in airport development, management and master-planning projects at more than 60 airports in over 20 countries.

The group also implements advanced digital solutions, including biometric technologies and automation, and follows carbon-neutrality principles.

World.title: Tony Burke breaks silence on ex-ASIO agent's Bondi royal commission testimony
World.content:
A former ASIO agent who wants to give evidence to the Bondi royal commission can do so in open hearings, the Home Affairs minister says, meaning he does not need a visa to travel to Australia.

It is the first time Tony Burke has publicly addressed the man's intent to testify after previously denying his Australian visa request.

The former agent, known as Marcus, wants to give evidence about what he knew of the Bondi gunmen in the years before last December's terror attack.

He spent years infiltrating Islamic extremist groups in western Sydney, working as a paid source for domestic spy agency ASIO before his cover was blown.

Marcus met the Akrams when he infiltrated Sydney's Islamic State network for ASIO. (Four Corners: Sissy Reyes)

Marcus has repeatedly made a case to give evidence from within Australia, due both to the sensitivity of his evidence and the legal protections he gains from being on Australian soil.

The royal commission has previously held classified hearings to ensure it can take evidence on sensitive intelligence information.

Mr Burke told reporters this morning he had been advised any evidence Marcus gives can be heard in public and heard remotely.

"Mike Burgess, the director-general of ASIO, has advised and made clear to the royal commission that any evidence that would come from this particular individual is declassified," he said.

Ex-spy denied visa ahead of Bondi RC The man who previously warned ASIO about the Bondi gunmen will not be able to give sensitive and classified evidence at the Royal Commission into Antisemitism and Social Cohesion.

"He's happy for it to be given in a complete public forum. It could be given over the phone on (Microsoft) Teams. It could be given in any way that the individual wants."

The royal commission has previously reached out to Marcus, it stated it is "eager" to hear his evidence and work out the best means for that to take place.

He is currently living abroad and cannot reach an Australian embassy.

Separately, NSW Police has also reached out to the former agent seeking assistance with its own investigations into last December's shooting.

Marcus has expressed fears for his personal safety while living overseas. He has sought protection and resettlement in Australia in the past.

His first visa application was rejected on the grounds that immigration authorities did not believe he had a genuine intention to leave the country, and his second application remains pending.

Mr Burke said the applications have followed all the normal channels.

"The department has its normal processes in working out whether or not someone qualifies for a visa under the Migration Act, and there hasn't been interference with that process," he said.

"The department looks at the Migration Act, looks at the application, and makes their own decision."

Advocates maintain call for visa

Whistleblower advocates have continued to back Marcus' cause, arguing the safest place for the former agent to give evidence is on Australian soil.

Marcus has previously told the ABC's Four Corners about his interactions with the Bondi gunmen, Sajid and Naveed Akram.

He claims he warned ASIO about the Akrams years before the attack.

ASIO has described the former agent as disgruntled and unreliable, but Marcus has rejected the characterisations.

Gabriel Shipton, from the whistleblower advocacy group the Information Rights Project, said he is in danger abroad.

Tense exchange at royal commission The witness, a Sydney researcher, questioned Israel's right to exist and was quizzed on her views comparing zionism to violent extremism.

"The protections offered by the royal commission do not extend outside Australia," he said.

"Marcus continues to risk his safety and the safety of his family. He is willing to give evidence and again the government is not acknowledging the threats he is under from the associates of the Akrams."

The group has provided support to the former agent as he lives overseas.

Mr Shipton said he should be allowed to give his evidence within Australia.

"The government has left it up to Information Rights to keep one of its ex-employees safe after years of undercover service, and again the minister has shown they are not serious about hearing evidence that contradicts the facts given by the institution in his own ministry."

World.title: 'Bittersweet': Vulnerable moment becomes national prize-winning photo
World.content:
Melbourne artist Nathan Beard has won the $30,000 National Photographic Portrait Prize for a faceless and intimate portrait of his aunty recuperating after a major medical scare.

Beard captured the private moment while visiting the beloved matriarch, Mae Khong, in Thailand earlier this year.

"On this particular trip she had suffered a fall at home and I was the only one in the house with her," he said.

The winning photograph in the 2026 National Photographic Portrait Prize, titled Mae Khong, by Melbourne artist Nathan Beard. (Supplied: Nathan Beard)

" She insisted that evening, even after the shock of the event, to bathe herself, and to do so independently. "

The National Portrait Gallery's Director of Curatorial and Collection, Isobel Parker Philip, said the photograph conveyed fortitude and strength, coupled with fatigue and vulnerability.

"You can't see her face but that doesn't mean you don't have an emotional connection to her," she said.

"You might look at it and see one of your loved ones; you can read the many, many years of her life experiences in the frame."

Mae died in July, meaning she will never know of the prestigious accolade bestowed on her nephew.

"It is bittersweet being recognised for the award because it's sort of a final gift of hers to me," Beard said.

NghỉNghiêm (AttentionAt ease), 2025 by Phuong Nguyen Le, winner of the $3,000 First Time Finalist Award. (Supplied: Phuong Nguyen Le)

The multidisciplinary artist, who draws on his Australian-Thai heritage, said his aunty was an influential figure in fostering his sense of cultural pride and belonging.

"She always struggled with why I would find her such a captivating subject," Beard said.

" She always thought it was silly that someone would think her worthy of that sort of status. "

Alongside the $30,000 prize money, Beard will also receive $20,000 worth of camera equipment.

UNTITLED_ 01 (Series_ What Remains_), by Hussein Abdirahman Mohamud, depicts a Flemington public housing resident packing to leave her home after it was earmarked for demolition. (Supplied: Hussein Abdirahman Mohamud)

Moments of joy, humour, tenderness

The image is among 30 finalists selected in this year's National Photographic Portrait Prize from more than 1,000 entries.

The selection showcases a diverse array of styles and subjects, from moments of joy and humour to poignant and tender snapshots.

Sublim8 by Camille Perry, a finalist in the National Photographic Portrait Prize 2026. (Supplied: Camille Perry)

"It truly is a celebration of portraiture in its most expanded form," Ms Parker Philip said.

Phuong Nguyen Le won the $3,000 First Time Finalist Award for a portrait of his father, taken to mark the 50th anniversary of the end of the Vietnam War.

Earlier this week, Melbourne photographer Hussein Abdirahman Mohamud won the $3,000 Art Handlers' Award for his image of a Flemington public housing resident, packing to leave her home after it was earmarked for demolition.

Holding Space by Adam Edwards was a finalist in the National Photographic Portrait Prize 2026. (Supplied: Adam Edwards)

This National Photographic Portrait Prize was launched in 2007 and is open to emerging and established artists.

This year marks the final iteration of the competition in its current format, with a new prize model to be announced by the National Portrait Gallery in 2027.

Hanging alongside the 2026 show is a retrospective exhibition of almost two decades of finalists' work.

A portrait of actor David Howell by Ingvar Kenne was also a finalist. (Supplied: Ingvar Kenne)

It includes some famous faces, such as former prime minister Bob Hawke sipping a milkshake.

"Photography makes up about 57 per cent of our collection," Ms Parker Philip said.

"It's really important to the gallery and we're excited to support more photographers in the future."

World.title: Man accused of defrauding Indigenous community not of 'dishonest mind'
World.content:
Lawyers representing a man accused of defrauding money meant for an Indigenous community say his actions do not show a "dishonest mind" but a "best effort" to account for where the money went.

Ankumuthi traditional owner Larry Joe Woosup has been charged with two counts of fraud to a value of $30,000 or more each. He has pleaded not guilty.

During the trial this week, the District Court in Cairns heard Mr Woosup and another community member arranged a deal with a mining company over the right to mine bauxite on traditional lands a year after a separate deal with the community reached a stalemate.

Mr Woosup then set up trust accounts with two different banks for the Ankumuthi community, where he was the sole trustee.

The jury was told it was an undisputed fact that Mr Woosup then used the overdraft capacity on one account to transfer and withdraw $110,000 and deposited a cheque for $95,000 from the mining company into the other account, which was then also withdrawn.

The requirement for both trusts was for all money to be used for the benefit of the Ankumuthi community, the court was told.

The crown case

Crown prosecutor Christian Peters told the jury Mr Woosup's dishonesty had been set out in "black and white".

Christian Peters (right) has told the court of Mr Woosup's multiple cash withdrawals. (ABC Far North: Brendan Mounter)

He said Mr Woosup was well and truly aware of his role as trustee and had been receiving advice every step of the way.

Mr Peters highlighted the various cash withdrawals from the multiple trust accounts, as well as some of the records of expenditure, including the purchase of three cars and numerous accommodation expenses.

Mr Peters also questioned the responses Mr Woosup gave in a questionnaire for federal court proceedings, where he listed a total of $13,000 in a fortnight as "personal expenses" and multiple cash withdrawals, each up to $5,000 in value, as non-specific "Trust bills".

"What bills? What bills was the trust paying?" Mr Peters said.

He also referenced some of Mr Woosup's conduct in the years after the alleged fraud, where other members of the Ankumuthi community confronted him about rumours he had taken money meant for the community.

The trial is expected to conclude with Judge Joshua Treviño KC's final closing statement on Monday. (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

In one witness's recollection, Mr Woosup apologised and asked for forgiveness.

"That is an admission by him … that that money was not used for the principal purposes of that trust," Mr Peters said.

Mr Woosup's defence

Mr Woosup's defence barrister, Matt Jackson, told the court that when questions first started to be raised about where trust money was spent, Mr Woosup engaged an accountant and provided bank statements and receipts.

Mr Jackson suggested to the jury that this was a "pretty good effort" to engage with the process and indicated an "honest state of mind".

He said the prosecution had an issue with Mr Woosup's use of cash and said while Mr Peters had asserted the purpose would be to defy tracing, Mr Jackson insisted it was not uncommon for Mr Woosup to pay bills in cash.

Mr Jackson also questioned if the prosecution had truly provided any evidence the money had not gone back to the community.

He said the cars purchased had been used for cultural surveys on country, and that many of the witnesses called who said they had not received any money only became recognised as Native Title holders years after the events.

Larry Joe Woosup has pleaded not guilty to two counts of fraud to a value of $30,000 or more each. (ABC Far North: Holly Richardson)

The jury heard from Mr Jackson that the many errors in Mr Woosup's documentation were evidence of the passage of time, rather than dishonesty.

"This case is not about what the trust means … it's about what Larry Woosup meant," Mr Jackson said.

He said his conduct, including his denials and apologies to members of the Ankumuthi community after the events, was also consistent with the state of mind that he did not do anything wrong.

"People can apologise for a number of different reasons … it doesn't mean they're trying to hide," Mr Jackson said.

Judge Joshua Treviño KC has begun his summing up to the jury and will continue when court resumes on Monday.

World.title: Jury discharged in rape trial of competitive bull rider
World.content:
The jury in the rape trial of competitive bull rider Clay Benjamin Hall has been discharged after failing to reach a verdict on one of two charges in relation to an incident in Warwick in 2021.

After more than eight hours of deliberations the jury unanimously found Mr Hall not guilty of one count of rape but was unable to reach a verdict on a second count related to the same incident.

Justice Philip McCarthy KC discharged the jury today after it failed to reach a unanimous or majority verdict on the remaining charge.

The court was told Mr Hall met the girl, who was in her late teens at the time, on a street in Warwick, about 160 kilometres south-west of Brisbane, in the early hours of October 2021.

Prosecutors alleged Mr Hall, now 26, raped the teenager after she offered to show him a shortcut to the Warwick Showgrounds.

The court heard the teenager had been drinking and had been at a house party with people she did not know before she met Mr Hall.

Clay Benjamin Hall told police in 2023 that he had been given consent by the complainant. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

Mr Hall was in Warwick to watch his brother compete at the Warwick Rodeo.

The court heard Mr Hall, who was not competing because of an injury, had also been drinking before walking to a service station to buy food in the early hours of the morning.

A key issue at trial was whether the sexual activity between Mr Hall and the complainant was consensual.

Defence barrister David Jones KC told the jury it was not in dispute that Mr Hall and the complainant had vaginal intercourse but rejected the allegation that anal penetration had occurred.

Jurors were shown a recording of a 2023 police interview in which Mr Hall said he propositioned the teenager and initially received no response but later he claimed was given consent.

The jury was also shown police interviews conducted with the complainant at hospital on the morning of the incident and later that day at a police station.

The complainant gave evidence during the trial and was cross-examined by the defence.

During deliberations jurors asked to view the complainant's recorded interviews again.

After more than eight hours of deliberations, Justice McCarthy gave the jury a majority verdict direction, allowing it to return a verdict if 11 jurors agreed and one disagreed.

But the jury later indicated it was unable to reach a majority verdict.

While discharging the jury, Justice McCarthy thanked jurors for their work.

"Whilst you may have a frustration, you worked very hard. Your endeavour was appreciated and I appreciated the way you took upon your task in this courtroom," he said.

The unresolved charge remains before the court and the matter will return to the Warwick District Court for a callover on September 17.

World.title: Prominent harness racing stable fined over insurance policy failure
World.content:
A prominent Tasmanian harness racing operator has been fined $8,000 for failing to secure adequate insurance, which came to light after employees were injured in a car crash that killed four horses.

Ben Yole Racing Pty Ltd was sentenced in the Launceston Magistrates Court this afternoon, after pleading guilty to failing to maintain a policy of insurance with a licensed insurer, between July 2022 and December 12, 2023.

The issue emerged after a car crash near Sidmouth in January 2023, where four horses were killed, and injured workers later learned they were not covered by workers' compensation insurance.

The company had more than 30 employees at the time.

Five Yole workers, who were aged between 14 and 20 at the time, were in the car at the time of the crash. (Facebook: The Vigilante News)

The prosecution had suggested the fine could have reached $90,500, while defence barrister Damian Sheales had argued a fine of between $1,500 and $2,500 would have been sufficient.

Magistrate Sharon Cure ordered the company to pay $62,168 to the WorkCover Tasmania Board and fined it $8,000 plus $82 in costs.

The driver crashed a vehicle towing a horse float after working for more than 18 hours, a court heard. (ABC News: Jess Moran)

Magistrate Cure made the point that the case had been dragging on for a long time and agreed with a comment from Mr Sheales that "everyone feels exhausted by it".

She said she accepted the company became aware that it did not have adequate insurance and took steps to address it.

She did not believe the breach stemmed from an attempt to gain an advantage over competitors.

While she said she gave some weight to the nature of work and level of risk its employees faced, she said the legislation does not take those factors into account.

The company was granted a stay of 28 days to make arrangements.

Ben Yole Racing faces further charges relating to failing its workplace health and safety duties, failing to report an incident, and failing to preserve an incident site, to which it previously pleaded not guilty.

These matters will return to court later this year.

World.title: Teenage boy charged with alleged murder of 13-year-old girl fronts court
World.content:
A Children's Court judge has said there are reasonable grounds to suggest a teenage boy committed the murder of a 13-year-old Wimmera girl.

The 16-year-old boy fronted a Children's Court of Victoria on Friday by video link from youth prison.

He is accused of murdering Layla Jeffery, whose body was found in bushland on July 9 after being reported missing from Donald, near Horsham, on July 5.

Judge Jack Vandersteen, the president of the children's court, said: "[The accused has] been charged as a single person and therefore as the principal."

He said there were reasonable grounds to believe the accused committed the offence, and that an item believed to have been at the scene of the alleged offending had been found.

Flowers adorn Layla Jeffery's memorial at the Bullocks Head lookout in Donald. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

Order for swabs

Judge Vandersteen granted a police application to get a new DNA sample from the accused, after chief crown prosecutor Kristie Churchill KC asked for the boy's previous sample to be destroyed.

The judge informed the teenage defendant that if he did not comply with the mouth swab, police could use reasonable force to obtain it.

"They will ask you to do it yourself and if you don't, they will do it," the judge said.

The accused replied: "Alright."

When asked if he had any questions for the judge, the accused said: "No, your honour."

Slouched, yawning

The accused attended his court appearance wearing a black beanie and a black T-shirt layered over a white long-sleeve top, with Judge Vandersteen asking him to remove the beanie at the start of the hearing.

After doing so, the teenager slouched down with his elbows on his knees for the rest of the hearing — periodically stretching, yawning and looking up at the camera.

The case has been adjourned until September 10.

World.title: Giant cuttlefish population down by 97pc, SA count shows
World.content:
South Australia's Department of Primary Industries and Regions (PIRSA) says giant cuttlefish numbers are down by 97 per cent.

Last year the department counted 63,000 cuttlefish in the Spencer Gulf waters. This year 1,811 were recorded.

South Australian Research and Development Institute executive director Professor Mike Steer said the decline was being monitored closely.

"The [giant cuttlefish] population has depleted and has likely been impacted by the algal bloom," he said.

The number is the lowest since 2013, when Pirsa recorded 13,000.

Marine biologists visited the Spencer Gulf last month to count the eggs left behind.

"Along that 8 kilometres of coastline we only found 440 eggs," Manny Katz said.

Clusters of giant cuttlefish eggs seen in the waters of the Spencer Gulf in 2025. (Supplied: Eyre Lab)

The annual gathering near Whyalla is one of the only known mass-breeding aggregations of its kind.

"It's the only place where our giant cuttlefish come for breeding," SA Climate, Environment and Water Minister Emily Bourke said.

"So we see this population as a priority to protect."

Emily Bourke says the government is aware of the significance of the species. (Supplied: Emily Bourke)

The future of the giant cuttlefish

Adult giant cuttlefish die shortly after spawning, leaving the next generation reliant on that single winter event.

"Normally when there's tens of thousands of cuttlefish and each female is laying dozens of eggs, you would expect there to be millions along the coastline," Mr Katz said.

Whyalla Dive Shop owner and Eyre Lab director Manny Katz. (Supplied: Manny Katz)

"My team went out and jammed our heads under every single rock we could at eight sites. At some we found no eggs at all.

"It's incredibly worrying. It's probably an indicator that next year's population is going to be incredibly low as well."

Professor Steer said the one-two year life cycle of the species gave cause for hope.

"In 2013 when numbers dropped down they popped back up in a couple of years," he said.

"Cuttlefish breed one year, die, and then the resulting hatchlings make up the population next year."

Mike Steer says giant cuttlefish populations can bounce back quickly. (ABC News: Dean Faulkner)

Professor Steer said the harmful algal bloom was a likely cause of the decline.

"We saw those [giant cuttlefish] eggs successfully hatch last year," he said.

"Those went into the water where the bloom was present, where we'd expect to see those juveniles and sub-adults. So it's likely that it's had an impact.

"We did see a lot of fish perish as a result of the algal bloom. We need to research into the food web structure."

Mr Katz is urging the government to protect the giant cuttlefish with a formal endangered listing.

"They should be listed as an endangered species," he said.

Giant cuttlefish at Stoney Point, near Whyalla. (Supplied: Carl Charter)

Invertebrates Australia has made an application for the species to be listed on the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List of Threatened Species.

"I think now there's reason to warrant them being federally listed in Australia as an endangered species, to trigger more funding and monitoring for the future," Mr Katz said.

A spokesperson for the federal government said in a statement that "the reduction in giant Australian cuttlefish populations in the Spencer Gulf is very concerning".

The spokesperson said Environment and Water Minister Murray Watt has asked that the Threatened Species Scientific Committee "urgently consider whether a listing for the Upper Spencer Gulf population of giant cuttlefish under the EPBC Act is appropriate, and if so, to undertake that assessment".

A joint research project between the state government and Adelaide University will track the Spencer Gulf giant cuttle fish population until 2028.

Research is also being conducted on how cuttlefish numbers are calculated.

That will be funded with part of the federal and state governments' $165 million algal bloom response fund.

World.title: Five of the best Sydney homes where past meets present
World.content:
PropertyNewsLuxury property Five of the best Sydney homes where past meets present Shona Hendley August 21, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Renovated period homes, showcasing timeless details and updated with modern features for contemporary living, can be rich in history and offer standout living options. From updated Victorian terraces to a beachside weatherboard cottage, here are five of the best Sydney homes where past meets present, all on the market now. 42 Jeffreys Street, Kirribilli, NSW This extensively updated Victorian terrace spans four levels within a harbourside enclave in Kirribilli.



Period features – including the facade, arched verandas and ornate cast-iron balustrade – welcome you while, inside, the formal dining room with its original marble fireplace and ceiling rose also showcases the home’s heritage. Modern renovations include the Calacatta Viola marble kitchen, marble-finished bars, and marble finishes throughout the four bedrooms, including the master suite with a walk-in wardrobe and en suite. Other standout features include the cellar and the top-floor bedroom with its own bathroom and balcony offering city skyline and Harbour Bridge views. 12 Cliff Street, Watsons Bay, NSW



This c1860 double-fronted weatherboard cottage, once home to the harbour master and later to Australian artist John Olsen, is just 300 metres from Camp Cove Beach. The renovated five-bedroom residence blends vintage and contemporary design, with 3.4-metre-high ceilings, lime-washed floorboards, a chef’s kitchen with a stone breakfast island, a walk-in pantry, and bursts of colour throughout the light-filled interiors. The property also includes a lower-level media retreat or a fifth bedroom and, outside, a courtyard and a bougainvillea-framed deck. 12 Findlay Avenue, Roseville, NSW



This Federation-era residence on an approximately 1477-square-metre block near Roseville Village is set for auction on Saturday, September 12. The original double-brick facade, vast proportions, fireplaces and high ceilings showcase the original design, while extensive updates introduce a contemporary aesthetic. Spacious open-plan living includes a high-end kitchen with Carrara splash backs, plus two additional family rooms for additional flexibility. Outside, there are established, manicured gardens, large lawns and a swimming pool. 86 Kenneth Street, Longueville NSW



Located on a dual-fronted block opposite Kingsford Smith Oval stands one of Longueville’s original homes. “Riverslea” was built c1885 and still retains much of its Victorian heritage, with high ceilings and fireplaces set within black-and-white marble mantles. The light-filled kitchen has been updated with marble benchtops and Smeg appliances, and bifold doors open to an undercover verandah overlooking the backyard, which features a 10-metre saltwater swimming pool. Set over two levels, the upper bedroom offers views of the Harbour Bridge, while a detached studio/garage could be converted into a granny flat, subject to council approval.



13 Baker Street, Kensington, NSW The original tessellated-tile entry and repointed frontage welcome you to this renovated Federation home. The contemporary rear extension features a double-height, open-plan living space that connects to a resort-style outdoor area with a covered entertaining area featuring an outdoor kitchen and an integrated barbecue, overlooking the landscaped gardens, lawn and a pool. Other features include hardwood floors, a north aspect, a skylit bathroom and an upstairs room that can serve as a sixth bedroom or rumpus room. The property is close to Moore Park and public transport.

World.title: Border force asked to seize fake squishies as demand surges
World.content:
Schylling’s ultimate owner, listed US-based private equity company Gladstone Investment Corporation, also invests in an American defence company that says: “The United States and its allies must be ready to fight and win – anywhere, anytime.”

This masthead can reveal that Schylling, the US company that manufactures NeeDoh, and its licensed Australian distributor, William Valentine, have approached Australian Border Force, raided factories in China and issued cease-and-desist letters to retailers selling fakes as they try to stop an influx of fake squishies coming in “thick and fast”.

Several children globally, including a 10-year-old Australian girl, have reported serious injuries from squishies exploding and burning them, and now NeeDoh’s manufacturer is facing a US class action alleging it failed to warn consumers about the risks of the toys when exposed to heat.

The gel-like cubes, dumplings and assorted fruit – all “squishies”, which kicked off from the original and most popular brand, NeeDoh – have children obsessed. Parents are baffled. But with viral popularity comes increasing scrutiny. What’s in the toys? Are they safe?

Australia’s Border Force has been asked to seize fake NeeDoh toys, as its manufacturer takes extraordinary steps to stop a barrage of dupes copying the global children’s squishy toy craze from flooding the local market.

Dyson says “every single primary-aged kid or teenager, they want one, and they are harassing their parents, the stores, the staff to get one. It is next level. Some of the messages we have received have been out of control – begging for NeeDohs.” She’s had people come to her shop from as far as Darwin trying to get NeeDohs.

“Everyone is just obsessed with them,” says Katie Hennessey, a Brisbane-based 18-year-old who has amassed more than 200,000 followers on TikTok with posts showing her unboxing squishies. “I don’t know why – they come in so many fun textures, shapes and colours. You want to collect all the different textures … which just makes it really fun.”

In early 2026, Schylling released an advent-calendar-style multipack – and the toys suddenly became viral hits.

Then, in January, “it just went absolutely mental,” recalls Adele Dyson, owner of Adventure Awaits in the northern Victorian town of Numurkah. “We sold a thousand units in like two days.”

Squishies have probably been around since humans learnt to work with the sap of the rubber tree. In a simpler age, kids filled balloons with rice to make malleable balls. Now, thanks to the modern chemical industry, squishies come in all shapes and varieties: blue, green, soap, chicken. Schylling, the 51-year-old Massachusetts-based toy maker, launched NeeDoh in 2017 , and the toy sold reasonably well.

While NeeDohs remain elusive, Schylling and its Australian distributor, William Valentine, have gone to great lengths to halt dupes from undercutting their brand and sales.

”We got a whole barrage of emails from parents saying ‘I’ve got three kids … my daughter is dying of cancer, send me NeeDohs’,” says Dyson. “One kid sent me 50 messages in one day: ‘give me NeeDoh. I have to have it’.”

And when a pallet last arrived at Dyson’s shop, it sold out online in four minutes, despite a limit of one per customer.

Google search volume for NeeDoh is up 2800 per cent on 2025, and “squishie” is up 5000 per cent. Some schools have had to ban the toys because kids were spending too long trading them, says Hennessey.

Jumping on the trend, other brands produce squishies too, including Smooshos Mystery Dumplings and Mushykinz Jelleez, which are also popular.

Schylling has been struggling to get new stock out to retailers. A pop-up on its website says it has closed its own online store. “Demand for NeeDoh and our other products is exceptionally high right now, so we’re taking a short pause on new orders.”

As well, retailers were told a “notice of objection form” is being lodged with Australian Border Force.

“This one is obviously a game of whack-a-mole due to the sheer scale of factories in China.”

“Last month they conducted raids on 11 counterfeit factories in unison, confiscating millions of fake units, machines, cash and in turn shutting down the factory in the process.

“Schylling is working closely with their Chinese trademark attorney and the Chinese consulate to do factory raids on any offenders,” the email states.

Business owners were told Schylling and William Valentine are “running a three-pronged approach” to stop the flood of dupes.

An email sent in June to retailers stocking NeeDoh, seen by this masthead, said: “Counterfeit product and websites are coming through thick and fast for NeeDoh.”

It’s a similar story in Preston, in Melbourne’s north, where Kid Stuff employee Emily Oppedisano said the squishies craze started at the end of last year.

“A lot of younger people come here and ask me about the squishies, and then recently dumpling squishies are really popular,” she said. “It’s a blind box, so … let’s say, [the] customer wants to get pink, but when they open it, it’s not pink, so they want to buy more until they get a pink one.”

At Mint My Desk in Parramatta, in Sydney’s west, worker Kai Takakura said squishies have become popular due to TikTok.

There are also plans to send “cease-and-desist” letters to stop retailers from selling fake NeeDoh products, and Schylling has urged business owners to dob in any outlets doing do.

“I’m currently lodging documentation with Australian Customs which allows them to seize goods at the Australian border for any importer other than us,” the email states. “This should also drastically slow down any of this product reaching the stores.”

“[NeeDoh products] were constantly selling out. They were selling out within two hours when we got them in,” she said.

She said there is a limit of one or two squishies per person, as children come through the doors and ask when stocks will be replenished.

Kids Stuff workers Shivani Kalra (left) and Emily Oppedisano (right) report NeeDoh stocks have been sold out for two months. Ruby Alexander

Alexander Mazniovski, 11, was buying a squishy from Toyworld at Northland shopping centre in Preston with his dad Tony Mazniovski this week. “They are fun to play with when you’re bored. They are all over social media,” he said.

His dad said the toys are also a “calming tool”, particularly for his other son, who has autism. “They serve more than one purpose,” Mazniovski said. “They serve him well when he is overloaded with different emotions.”

Alexander Mazniovski, 11, buys a squishy from Toyworld with his dad Tony, who says the toys can be used as “calming” tools. Ruby Alexander

Toyworld moved to place the bulk of their squishy stock behind the counter, due to the swarms of kids coming in wanting to touch and play with them. Instead, they have installed a “demo box” in front of the counter.

Melbourne mother of two, Elena, said her daughters Audrey, 9, and Vanessa, 6, have both requested squishies for their birthdays in October and November. “They are taking over my household,” said Elena, who requested her last name remain private. Her elder daughter trades them with her cousin, so they can play with new shapes.

Elena says she is conscious of safety when it comes to the toys, and has paid for the more expensive squishies in the hope that they are not toxic. She also insists on buying the branded toys.

“We try to get the premium dumpling [squishies]. We have ordered a mega dumpling from an Australian store in Queensland, on the understanding it is the real deal. I’m not comfortable with buying them on Amazon,” she said.

Vanessa and Audrey’s parents take care to buy branded squishies, and avoid the cheaper models. Eddie Jim

Are they safe?

Seven-year-old Hinata Morris loves squishies – she already has nine and is hoping to get more – but there’s been a recent change that has made her and her parents cautious about purchasing the viral toys: a strong chemical smell.

“There’s a little bit of fear of all the soft ones, so now we’re always smelling things before we buy,” Hinata’s father, Brendan Morris, said.

Hinata Morris’ parents have noticed an increase in fake squishies being sold at places like market stalls or service stations. Sitthixay Ditthavong

The family, who lives in Cobbitty in Sydney’s south-west, said they’ve noticed an increase in fake squishies being sold across Sydney at places like market stands and at the front of petrol stations. Morris said he once bought a squishy toy for Hinata and, on his way out of the store, squeezed it and it immediately popped.

“It can be really easy to buy one and then be really nervous later that it doesn’t smell right,” he said. “It just makes us really aware of where we buy them from and, where possible, buying the better brands just to have a bit more peace of mind.”

In June, 10-year-old Gold Coaster Violet Zerbst placed her NeeDoh Nice Cube in the microwave for a few seconds. She pulled the warm cube out, gave it a squish – and then it exploded in her hands, covering her face with red-hot goo.

Violet spent a week in hospital with superficial burns across her face. “It’s a toffee-like substance, it was scolding and sticky and it stuck to her face,” her father Jody Zerbst told The Gold Coast Bulletin. “All the skin had sort of peeled off – it was really gruesome.”

Violet is one of several children globally injured by hot, exploding squish-toys.

US-based Consumer Reports in 2025 found some squishies reached almost 95 degrees Celsius and exploded after just 15 seconds in a microwave.

Schylling now warns on its website against heating or microwaving NeeDoh. But a NeeDoh Nice Cube obtained by this masthead only warns against leaving the product in the car or direct sun.

NeeDoh is no longer the only player. As the toys have exploded in popularity, counterfeits and knock-offs have followed.

In a shop in Parramatta, squishy fan Girlie Agaran points out which of the toys in front of her are fake and real. When asked how she can spot the difference, she shrugs and says it can be hard to tell. The fake toys are more affordable, and now more available, than the real ones, Agaran said.

Squishy fan Girlie Agaran says it can be hard to pick the real thing from the fakes. Sitthixay Ditthavong

“Some of my squishies are from Shein, it’s quite cheap there … but there’s a lot of places like malls. They put up pop-up shops and they just sell NeeDoh’s for $10, $5,” she said.

In 2018, Denmark’s Environmental Protection Agency tested eight “squishie” toys, finding about 100 different chemicals in each, mostly a range of plastics and fragrances. Several of these were at high enough concentrations that prolonged exposure – like sleeping with a squishie, or keeping a large number in a small room – could cause irritation, the agency found.

Australian testing by consumer protection agencies in South Australia and Western Australia found much lower levels of chemicals, and they were “unlikely to pose a risk”, spokespeople told this masthead.

Still, Kidsafe advises parents to sniff their squishies. “Avoid any squishy toy that exhibits a strong chemical odour, an oily residue, or visible damage such as cracks, punctures, or leaks,” said Kidsafe Victoria chief executive Sarah Sexton.

This masthead purchased a range of squishies from Northland shopping centre. Some came in boxes with warnings not to leave them in direct sun. Some came with choking-hazard warnings. A squishable Jumbo Duck came in a plastic bag with only a warning about being given to children under three. None, other than the NeeDoh, declared what they were made of.

“That one most definitely smells like chemicals. It smells like you’re at a petrol station,” said Professor Blair Kuys, a consultant toy designer and executive dean of Swinburne University’s School of Design and Architecture, upon getting a whiff of the Jumbo Duck.

When this masthead sliced off Jumbo Duck’s head with a knife, a thick white cream smelling strongly of petrol came oozing out. “Looks gross,” said Kuys. “It may be some type of gel that, I doubt, would comply with safety standards.”

Warnings listed on squishy products. Ruby Alexander

The warning labels on the boxes were so small that Kuys struggled to read them. Jumbo Duck has almost no warning labels at all, and comes in “a plastic bag you can choke on”.

“I don’t feel good about the production quality,” he said. “My biggest concern is a young kid stretching it open, bursting it, and eating it.”

The makers of NeeDoh argue those concerns don’t apply to their products, which are made of a thermoplastic rubber skin encasing different fillings, including polyvinyl alcohol (a type of plastic), maltose (a sugar), or cornstarch.

“I have no idea what malt extract is doing in plastic toys,” said Adelaide University molecular pharmacologist Dr Ian Musgrave. “It’s a food, generally recognised as safe. It’s basically concentrated sugar syrup. I wouldn’t eat if it leaked out, though.”

A class action

NeeDoh toys are manufactured by US toy company Schylling. Schylling’s parent is also US-based private equity investment company Gladstone Investment Corporation.

Gladstone Investment Corporation is listed on the NASDAQ, and acquired Schylling in 2013 in a deal that saw it partner with another private equity company Crofton Capital.

According to the latest full-year results for Gladstone in the year to March 31, Schylling is one of the company’s key investments.

Gladstone’s investment portfolio is made up of 29 companies with an aggregate value of $US1.3 billion ($1.83 billion). It is also invested in other industries like defence. In 2024, Gladstone acquired Detroit Defense, an engineering and logistics provider that “empower(s) the warfighter”.

It does not explicitly say it is a weapons manufacturer, but says it provides “systems engineering, systems integration, and integrated logistics services to the US Department of Defense and its allies”.

Schylling is listed as one of five of Gladstone’s “largest portfolio investments”. Collectively, they comprise $US582.6 million, or 44.5 per cent, of the company’s total investment portfolio at fair value as of March 31, 2026, their latest results reported.

According to its latest results, Gladstone valued its stake in Schylling at $US66.4 million in equity in the year to March 31. It’s up from $US20.5 million in the previous year to March 31, 2025.

Despite Schylling’s positive financial results – probably buoyed by the viral NeeDoh products – the company was hit with a class action in the US in late July.

Lead plaintiff Cristiana Mendoza alleged a NeeDoh Nice Cube exploded when she squeezed it and expelled “extremely hot inside filler” onto her leg.

“The NeeDoh did not feel hot to touch, but exploded when she squeezed it and expelled extremely hot inside filler onto plaintiff’s leg, burning her and causing blistering, painful red skin and irritation,” she alleged in her lawsuit filed in the northern district of California.

Her complaint alleged Schylling’s warnings are incomplete, and don’t provide adequate storage instructions. The class action is seeking compensation and an order that Schylling should “conspicuously disclose the risks”.

Mendoza, a behavioral technician who works with autistic children, alleged the cube was inside on her TV stand near a window when she picked it up on May 15 this year.

It had not been microwaved or frozen.

“A reasonable purchaser of a child-oriented sensory toy does not expect that leaving it indoors near a window, in a car, in a classroom, or in another foreseeable location may convert the toy into a pressurised container capable of rupturing and expelling dangerously hot, adhesive filling,” she alleged.

Schylling has warned the products may become hot if left in a car or in direct sunlight, and informed consumers heating, freezing or microwaving can cause personal injury.

The court documents report the “proposed class action contains at least 100 members”, but the exact number is not known because incident complaints, returns and insurance claims are controlled by Schylling and third parties, according to the claim.

Schylling was contacted for comment by this masthead with questions about the safety of their products and if they intend to defend the class action. The company did not respond before deadline.
